newsitem.title: GERMANY: Court convicts East German spymaster Wolf.
newsitem.headline: Court convicts East German spymaster Wolf.

text.p: Former East German spymaster Markus Wolf was found guilty in a German court on Tuesday of three kidnappings during the Cold War and handed a two year suspended sentence.
The trial was the latest and possibly last attempt to punish the man who ran East Germany's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years after a 1993 treason conviction was overturned in 1995.

Wolf was charged with organising the kidnapping in 1959 of a Ministry for State Security (Stasi) official who had fled to West Germany and the abduction of a West Berlin secretary whom the authorities hoped to persuade to spy for the East.
Prosecutors said Wolf, 74, was also behind the arrest of an East German whom the Stasi tried to force to take part in a plot against former Chancellor Willy Brandt, then mayor of West Berlin.
Prosecutors said Wolf engineered all three abductions and accused him of coercion, causing injury and kidnapping and had demanded a three-and-a-half year jail sentence for him.
Wolf denied all the charges and had said he was being punished by what he called a political trial as a substitute for bringing to book former communist East German leaders.
Wolf was convicted of treason in the same Duesseldorf courtroom in 1993. But the conviction was overturned in 1995.
This time prosecutors charged Wolf with crimes under East German law and three weeks ago dropped charges of treason and extortion against him to speed up the trial.

The elusive figure, who ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters, was dubbed "the man without a face" by his Western counterparts, who for decades had little idea what he looked like.
Thriller writers often took him as a model when depicting a sinister communist spy chief.
One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside then chancellor Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
